transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because I just can’t shake this feeling that work isn’t safe anymore. And I feel like something in me is… damaged now. Like the person who was competent, who got promoted, isn’t really there the same way anymore.
Do you feel anxious most of the time?

Yes. It’s like I’m almost always on alert. On the train, in meetings, even at lunch with my team, I’m checking where the exits are, watching if someone is standing too close, listening for noises in the hallway. I’m there, but I’m not really fully present.
Have you been avoiding certain places or situations because of these feelings?

Yes. I’ve been changing my shifts when I can, and I keep pushing back on release windows if they mean I’d be there late. I also take the side entrance now, or work from home whenever it’s possible, because walking through the lobby after dark just… it feels like I’m going to fall apart.
Has something specific and disturbing happened to you at work or somewhere else that's making you feel this way?

Yes. There was an incident at work. I don’t really like talking about it, but certain things bring it back hard — like a badge scanner beeping, or heavy footsteps in the hallway, or a late-night deployment alert. Suddenly I’m back in that office again, and my chest gets tight, and I see the guard on the floor. It cuts through whatever I’m doing.
Have you been feeling sad or hopeless most of the time since the incident happened?
I don’t know that I’d say sad or hopeless most of the time. I’ve felt really shaken and worn down, but I haven’t really been tracking it as sadness exactly.
Do you ever find yourself reliving the incident at work as if it were happening again?

Yes. Not all the time, but certain sounds can do it — the badge scanner beeping, heavy footsteps in the hallway, or a late-night deployment alert. It’s like I’m suddenly back in that office, and my chest gets tight, and I see the guard on the floor again. It cuts into whatever I’m doing.
Do you try to avoid thinking about the incident at work?

Yes. I try not to think about it, and I’ve changed a lot of what I do to avoid being reminded. I’ve been trading shifts, pushing back release windows, and using the side entrance or working from home when I can. Walking through that lobby after dark just makes me feel like I’m going to come apart.
Do you ever feel like you're outside of your body, watching yourself?
I’m not sure. I don’t think I’ve noticed that specifically—like watching myself from the outside. Mostly I just feel really overwhelmed in the moment, but not exactly outside my body.
Do you ever feel numb or disconnected from the world around you?

I don’t know. I don’t think I’d describe it that way, exactly. Sometimes I feel kind of checked out or quiet after I get upset, but I haven’t really noticed feeling disconnected from everything around me.
Do you avoid talking to people who were present during the incident at work?

Yes. I mean, I don’t go out of my way to talk to them. I’ve been trading shifts and pushing release windows so I don’t have to be there with the same people, and if I can work from home or use the side entrance, I do. It’s mostly about not having to go through that lobby after dark, but I guess it also keeps me from dealing with anyone who was there.
Do you feel guilty about what happened during the incident at work?

Yes. I keep going over it and thinking if I had pushed harder for better security during the overnight deployment, or if I’d called for help sooner, maybe the guard wouldn’t have been hurt so badly. I know I was scared and hiding, but I still feel like I should’ve done something different.
Have you lost interest in activities that you used to enjoy?

Yes. I used to be pretty involved outside my regular work — mentoring newer people, going to women-in-tech events, that kind of thing. Lately I’ve pulled back from most of it because I don’t feel steady or reliable enough.

Even my actual work has slipped. I’ve missed migration deadlines and avoided late deployments I normally would’ve handled. It’s gotten bad enough that it came up in a performance review, including conflicts that didn’t used to happen.
Have you noticed a decrease in your interest in activities that were once important to you since the incident?

Yes. Since then, I’ve pulled back from things that used to matter to me, like mentoring and women-in-tech events. I just don’t feel steady or reliable enough to take that on right now.

And at work, it’s affected me too. I’ve missed migration deadlines, avoided late deployments I normally would’ve handled, and it even came up in my performance review because of conflicts that didn’t used to happen.
Has your relationship with family or friends been affected by how you've been feeling since the incident?
I’m not really sure. I mean, I’ve probably been more withdrawn than usual, but I can’t point to anything specific with my family or friends that’s clearly changed because of it.
Have you had difficulty performing your job or maintaining relationships because of these feelings and experiences?

Yes. My job has definitely been affected. I’ve missed migration deadlines and avoided some late deployments I normally would’ve handled, and it was brought up in a performance review because of conflicts that didn’t used to happen.

With relationships, it’s more around work and professional stuff. I’ve pulled back from mentoring and women-in-tech leadership events because I don’t feel steady or reliable enough right now.
How long have you been experiencing these feelings and changes since the incident at work?
It’s been since the break-in during that overnight deployment… so about two years and four months now.
